results.title: Open coloring of a topological space
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: Let $X$ be a topological space. A set $K \subseteq X \times X$ of ordered pairs is an open coloring of $X$ if $K$ is open in the product topology, symmetric ($(x, y) \in K$ implies $(y, x) \in K$) and irreflexive ($(x, x) \notin K$ for every $x \in X$).

results.title: Homogeneous set for a coloring
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $X$ be a set and $K \subseteq X \times X$. A set $H \subseteq X$ is $K$-homogeneous if $(x, y) \in K$ for all distinct $x, y \in H$.

results.title: Free set for a coloring
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $X$ be a set and $K \subseteq X \times X$. A set $H \subseteq X$ is $K$-free if $(x, y) \notin K$ for all $x, y \in H$.

results.title: Open coloring axiom
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Todorcevic's Open Coloring Axiom: for every open coloring of a second-countable space, either there is an uncountable homogeneous set, or the space is a countable union of free sets.

results.title: Right-orderable group
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A group $G$ is right-orderable if it admits a linear order $\le$ that is invariant under right multiplication: $a \le b$ implies $ac \le bc$ for all $a, b, c \in G$.

results.title: Smallest run of six consecutive happy numbers
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A natural number is happy when repeatedly replacing it by the sum of the squares of its decimal digits reaches $1$ after finitely many steps. Let $N_0 = 7899999999999959999999996$. The six consecutive integers $N_0, N_0 + 1, \dots, N_0 + 5$ are all happy, and every natural number $m$ such that $m, m + 1, \dots, m + 5$ are all happy satisfies $m \ge N_0$.

For $b \le -2$, $T_b(f, a)$ is thus the sum of the squares of the first…

results.title: Sum of squared digits in a negative base
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $b \le -2$ be an integer. Every integer $a$ has an expansion $a = \sum_{i=0}^{n} a_i b^i$ with digits $0 \le a_i \le |b| - 1$, unique up to leading zero digits, and $S_{2,b}(a) = \sum_{i=0}^{n} a_i^2$ is the sum of the squares of these digits. The digits are produced from the least significant one by taking $a_0 = a \bmod b$ and passing to $(a - a_0)/b$, until $0$ is reached.

results.summary: There is an integer $n$ such that $n + 3i$ is $(-2)$-happy for every natural number $i$, and an integer $a$ is $(-2)$-happy if and only if $a \equiv 1 \pmod 3$.

results.title: Happy numbers in base $-3$

results.title: Goodness pulls back along compositions of the digit-square map and the successor map
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $b \le -2$ be an integer, let $S_{2,b}$ be the map sending an integer to the sum of the squares of its base-$b$ digits, and let $I(t) = t + 1$. Let $T$ be a finite set of positive integers and let $F$ be a composition $F = f_1 \circ \dots \circ f_m$ with $m \ge 0$ (the empty composition being the identity), where each $f_i$ is $S_{2,b}$ or $I$. If the image $F(T)$ is $(2, b)$-good, then $T$ is $(2, b)$-good.

results.title: A common iterate of the negative-base digit-square map falls below twice the squared base

For every finite set $A$ of positive integers there is an integer $k \ge 1$ such that $S_{2,b}^k(a) < 2b^2$ for every $a \in A$.

results.title: Cayley transform of an operator
results.caption: Definition

results.title: Spectral mapping for the Cayley transform, image direction
results.caption: Theorem

results.title: Spectral mapping for the Cayley transform, preimage direction
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The preimage direction of the spectral mapping: every point of the spectrum of `U` is `(w - i) / (w + i)` for some `w` in the spectrum of `A`.

results.title: Spectrum of the Cayley transform
results.caption: Theorem

results.title: Spectrum of the Cayley transform lies on the unit circle

results.title: Eigenvalues of the Cayley transform
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The eigenvalue correspondence: for `μ ≠ 1`, `μ` is an eigenvalue of the Cayley transform `U` iff `i * (1 + μ) / (1 - μ)` is an eigenvalue of `A`.

results.title: Velocities of curves in a level set lie in the kernel of the derivative
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $E$ be a real normed space, $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and $f : E \to \mathbb{R}$ a function differentiable at $x \in E$. If a curve $\gamma : \mathbb{R} \to E$ satisfies $\gamma(0) = x$, has derivative $v$ at $0$, and satisfies $f(\gamma(t)) = c$ for all $t \in \mathbb{R}$, then $Df(x)v = 0$.

results.title: Kernel vectors are velocities of local curves in a level set
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $E$ be a real Banach space and let $f : E \to \mathbb{R}$ have a strict derivative $f'$ at $x \in E$, a continuous linear map $E \to \mathbb{R}$ that is surjective. Then for every $v \in E$ with $f'(v) = 0$ there is a curve $\varphi : \mathbb{R} \to E$ with $\varphi(0) = x$ and $\varphi'(0) = v$ such that $f(\varphi(t)) = f(x)$ for all $t$ in some neighbourhood of $0$.

results.title: Kernel vectors are velocities of curves in a regular level set
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $E$ be a real Banach space, $f : E \to \mathbb{R}$ a $C^1$ function, $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and $x \in E$ a point with $f(x) = c$ at which the derivative $Df(x) : E \to \mathbb{R}$ is surjective. Then for every $v \in E$ with $Df(x)v = 0$ there is a curve $\gamma : \mathbb{R} \to E$ with $\gamma(0) = x$, $\gamma'(0) = v$ and $f(\gamma(t)) = c$ for all $t \in \mathbb{R}$.

results.title: Harris inequality
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The Harris inequality (Harris 1960): under the product Bernoulli(`p`) measure on a finite configuration space, increasing events are positively correlated, `P_p(A) * P_p(B) ≤ P_p(A ∩ B)`. No measurability hypothesis is needed since `E` is finite. See also `IsUpperSet.le_card_inter_finset` (Harris–Kleitman, counting form).

results.summary: OSSS inequality (O'Donnell, Saks, Schramm, Servedio, *Every decision tree has an influential variable*, FOCS 2005): if the decision tree `T` computes `f`, then `Var(f) ≤ ∑ᵢ δᵢ(T) Infᵢ(f)` under every product probability measure.

results.title: OSSS inequality
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: OSSS inequality, covariance form (O'Donnell, Saks, Schramm, Servedio, *Every decision tree has an influential variable*, FOCS 2005; in this form Duminil-Copin, Raoufi, Tassion, Ann. of Math. 2019): if the decision tree `T` computes the Boolean function `f`, then for every real function `g` and every product probability measure, `Cov(f, g) ≤ ∑ᵢ δᵢ(T) Infᵢ(g)`, where `Infᵢ(g) = 𝔼 |g(ω^{i ↦ 1}) - g(ω^{i ↦ 0})|`.

results.title: Poincaré inequality for Boolean functions under a product measure
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Poincaré inequality for Boolean functions under a product measure: `Var(1_A) ≤ ∑ₑ Infₑ(1_A)`, where `Infₑ(1_A)` is the probability that `e` is pivotal. This is the OSSS inequality for the full decision tree; it is weaker than the Efron–Stein inequality `Var(f) ≤ ∑ₑ pₑ(1 - pₑ) 𝔼[(∂ₑ f)²]` by the factor `pₑ(1 - pₑ) ≤ 1/4`.

results.title: Covariance form of the Poincaré inequality
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Covariance form of `poincare`: `Cov(1_A, g) ≤ ∑ₑ Infₑ(g)` for every real function `g`.

path: Designs, Latin squares and combinatorial matrices
Block-compatible sequences of pairwise balanced designs

results.title: Pairwise balanced design
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $n$, a finite list of blocks $B_1, \ldots, B_m \subseteq \{0, \ldots, n - 1\}$ is a pairwise balanced design on these $n$ points when the blocks are pairwise distinct, every block has at least two points, and every two distinct points lie in exactly one common block.

results.title: Block-compatible sequences
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $n$, a finite sequence $(x_1, \ldots, x_m)$ of natural numbers is block-compatible for $n$ when $x_1 \ge x_2 \ge \cdots \ge x_m$, every $x_k$ satisfies $2 \le x_k \le n$, and there is a pairwise balanced design on the point set $\{0, \ldots, n - 1\}$ whose blocks, listed in order as $B_1, \ldots, B_m$, have sizes $|B_k| = x_k$ for every $k$.

results.title: Many block-compatible sequences
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The statement that there are a real number $c > 0$ and a natural number $N$ such that for every $n \ge N$ there is a finite set of at least $\exp(c \sqrt{n} \log n)$ distinct finite sequences of natural numbers, each of which is block-compatible for $n$. Here $\log$ is the natural logarithm.

results.title: Many block-compatible sequences (Erdős Problem 732)
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: There are a real number $c > 0$ and a natural number $N$ such that for every $n \ge N$ there is a finite set of at least $\exp(c \sqrt{n} \log n)$ distinct finite sequences of natural numbers, each of which is block-compatible for $n$. Here $\log$ is the natural logarithm.

results.title: Erdős Problem 207
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The statement that for every integer $g \ge 2$ there is an $N$ such that for every $n \ge N$ with $n \equiv 1$ or $n \equiv 3 \pmod 6$ there is a Steiner triple system on the $n$ points $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ (three-point blocks, every pair of distinct points in exactly one block) in which every set of $j$ distinct blocks, with $2 \le j \le g$, covers at least $j + 3$ points.

results.title: Attainable sums in exact subset sum
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a list $x = (x_1, \dots, x_n)$ of natural numbers and a target $t \in \mathbb{N}$, this timed procedure starts from the list $L_0 = (0)$ and, for $i = 1, \dots, n$ in order, forms $L_i$ from $L_{i-1}$ in four steps: add $x_i$ to every entry of $L_{i-1}$; merge $L_{i-1}$ with this shifted list (the standard merge of two lists, comparing entries with $\le$); delete adjacent repeated values; and keep only the…

results.title: Characterization of the exact subset sum list
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $x$ be a list of natural numbers, $t$ a natural number, and $L$ the final list of sums computed by the exact subset sum traversal on $x$ with target $t$. A natural number $z$ belongs to $L$ if and only if $z \le t$ and $z$ is the sum of some sublist of $x$ (a subsequence, not necessarily contiguous).

results.title: Zero is always a computed sum
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $x$ of natural numbers and every natural number $t$, the final list of sums computed by the exact subset sum traversal on $x$ with target $t$ contains $0$.

results.title: The exact subset sum list is strictly increasing
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $x$ of natural numbers and every natural number $t$, the final list of sums computed by the exact subset sum traversal on $x$ with target $t$ is strictly increasing; in particular it has no repeated entries.

results.title: The number of computed sums is at most two to the power of the input length
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $x$ of natural numbers, of length $n$, and every natural number $t$, the final list of sums computed by the exact subset sum traversal on $x$ with target $t$ has length at most $2^n$.

results.title: The number of computed sums is at most the target plus one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $x$ of natural numbers and every natural number $t$, the final list of sums computed by the exact subset sum traversal on $x$ with target $t$ has length at most $t + 1$.

results.title: The number of computed sums is at most the input total plus one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $x$ of natural numbers with sum $S$ and every natural number $t$, the final list of sums computed by the exact subset sum traversal on $x$ with target $t$ has length at most $S + 1$.

results.title: Prefixes of the powers of two attain every sum
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $i \le n$ be natural numbers. On the list $1, 2, 4, \dots, 2^{i-1}$ (the first $i$ entries of $1, 2, \dots, 2^{n-1}$) with target $2^n - 1$, the final list of sums computed by the exact subset sum traversal is exactly $0, 1, 2, \dots, 2^i - 1$ in increasing order.

results.title: Exact subset sum procedure
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a list $x$ of natural numbers and a target $t \in \mathbb{N}$, the procedure first computes the list $L = (\ell_1, \dots, \ell_m)$ of attainable sums of $x$ with target $t$, then scans it from left to right, keeping a running maximum that starts at $0$, and returns $\max(0, \ell_1, \dots, \ell_m)$. Its counted events are those of computing $L$ plus one per entry of $L$.

results.title: Exact subset sum returns the maximum of the computed sums
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $x$ of natural numbers and every natural number $t$, the value returned by the exact subset sum algorithm on $x$ with target $t$ equals $\max(\cdots\max(\max(0, s_1), s_2)\cdots, s_k)$, where $s_1, \dots, s_k$ is the final list of sums computed by the exact subset sum traversal on $x$ with target $t$.

results.title: Event count of exact subset sum
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $x = (x_1, \dots, x_n)$ be a list of natural numbers and $t \in \mathbb{N}$ a target. For $0 \le i \le n$ let $L_i$ be the list of attainable sums of the prefix $(x_1, \dots, x_i)$ with target $t$. For $i < n$ let $M_i$ be the merge of $L_i$ with the list obtained by adding $x_{i+1}$ to every entry of $L_i$, let $c_i$ be the number of comparisons this merge makes, and let $D_i$ be $M_i$ with adjacent repeated…

results.title: Exponential lower bound for exact subset sum on powers of two
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the exact subset-sum procedure on the list $(2^0, 2^1, \dots, 2^{n-1})$ (empty when $n = 0$) with target $2^n - 1$ makes at least $2^n - 1$ counted events.

results.title: Exponential upper bound for exact subset sum
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $x$ of $n$ natural numbers and every target $t \in \mathbb{N}$, the exact subset-sum procedure on $x$ and $t$ makes at most $1 + n + 7(2^n - 1) + 2^n$ counted events.

results.title: Pseudo-polynomial bound for exact subset sum
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $x$ of $n$ natural numbers with sum $s$ and every target $t \in \mathbb{N}$, the exact subset-sum procedure on $x$ and $t$ makes at most $1 + n + (7n + 1)\min(t + 1, s + 1)$ counted events.

results.title: Polynomial event bound for exact subset sum with a polynomially bounded target
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $x$ be a list of $n$ natural numbers and let $t, d \in \mathbb{N}$ with $t \le n^d$. Then the exact subset-sum procedure on $x$ and $t$ makes at most $1 + n + (7n + 1)(n^d + 1)$ counted events.

results.title: Polynomial event bound for exact subset sum with polynomially bounded inputs
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $x$ be a list of $n$ natural numbers and let $d \in \mathbb{N}$ be such that every entry of $x$ is at most $n^d$. Then for every target $t \in \mathbb{N}$ the exact subset-sum procedure on $x$ and $t$ makes at most $1 + n + (7n + 1)(n \cdot n^d + 1)$ counted events.

results.title: Optimality of exact subset sum
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $x$ be a list of natural numbers, $t$ a natural number, and $r$ the value returned by the exact subset sum algorithm on $x$ with target $t$. Then $r$ is the sum of some sublist of $x$ (a subsequence, not necessarily contiguous), $r \le t$, and every sublist of $x$ whose sum is at most $t$ has sum at most $r$.

results.title: Optimality of exact subset sum for distinct positive inputs
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $x$ be a list of distinct positive natural numbers, $t$ a positive natural number, and $r$ the value returned by the exact subset sum algorithm on $x$ with target $t$. Then $r$ is the sum of some sublist of $x$ (a subsequence, not necessarily contiguous), $r \le t$, and every sublist of $x$ whose sum is at most $t$ has sum at most $r$.

results.title: Vector clock stamp of an event
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $P$ be the set of processes. Given the current vectors $V_q \in \mathbb{N}^P$ of the processes $q$ and the timestamps $T_0, T_1, \dots$ assigned so far, the vector clock algorithm stamps an event $e$ of process $p$ as follows. Let $m = T_i$ if $e$ receives the message sent by the event at position $i$ and $T_i$ has been assigned, and $m = 0$ otherwise. The stamp of $e$ is the pointwise maximum of $V_p$ and $m$,…

results.title: One step of the vector clock algorithm
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The state of the algorithm holds a vector $V_q \in \mathbb{N}^P$ for each process $q$, where $P$ is the set of processes, and the timestamps assigned so far, kept in an array for constant-time append and lookup. On an event $e$ of process $p$, the step replaces $V_p$ by the stamp $s$ of $e$ computed from the current state, leaves the other vectors unchanged, and appends $s$ to the timestamps.

results.title: Running the vector clock algorithm
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The state of the vector clock algorithm after an execution is obtained by starting from the state in which every process's vector is $0$ and no timestamps have been assigned, and applying one step of the algorithm to each event of the execution in order.

results.title: Vector timestamps of an execution
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The vector timestamps of an execution are the list of vectors that the vector clock algorithm, run over the execution, assigns to its events, in order.

results.title: Array lookup agrees with the timestamp list
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every execution and every natural number $i$, the entry at index $i$ of the array of timestamps built by the vector clock algorithm on the execution equals the $i$-th vector timestamp of the execution, where an index out of range gives the zero vector in both lookups.

results.title: Timestamps are stamps from the preceding state
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every execution and every position $j$ of an event $e$ of it, the vector timestamp of $j$ equals the stamp of $e$ computed from the state of the vector clock algorithm after the first $j$ events of the execution.

results.title: Each process's vector dominates its events' timestamps
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every execution and every position $i$ of an event of it, the vector timestamp of $i$ is pointwise at most the vector of that event's process in the state of the vector clock algorithm after the whole execution.

results.title: A process's final vector is zero or one of its timestamps
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Run the vector clock algorithm over an execution, starting from all vectors $0$. For every process $p$, the vector held by $p$ at the end is either the zero vector or the vector timestamp of some event of $p$ in the execution.

results.title: An event's own entry is positive
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every position $j$ of an event of an execution, if $p$ is the process of that event, then the $p$-entry of the vector timestamp of $j$ is at least $1$.

results.title: Vector timestamps are monotone along one step of happened-before
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In an execution, write $V_i$ for the vector timestamp that the vector clock algorithm gives to the event at position $i$. If the event at position $j$ follows the event at position $i$ by one step of happened-before, then $V_i(q) \le V_j(q)$ for every process $q$.

results.title: Vector timestamps are monotone along happened-before
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In an execution, write $V_i$ for the vector timestamp that the vector clock algorithm gives to the event at position $i$. If the event at position $a$ happened before the event at position $b$, then $V_a(q) \le V_b(q)$ for every process $q$.

results.title: Own-entry comparison detects happened-before
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $a$ and $b$ be positions of events of an execution, and let $p$ be the process of the event at $a$. If the $p$-entry of the vector timestamp of $a$ is at most the $p$-entry of the vector timestamp of $b$, then $a = b$ or $a$ happened before $b$.

results.title: Vector clocks characterize happened-before
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For two events of an execution, `a` happened before `b` exactly when `a`'s timestamp is smaller than `b`'s in the pointwise order.
